newsitem.title: MEXICO: Analysts downplay shift in Mexico monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Analysts downplay shift in Mexico monetary policy.

text.p: Economists on Monday downplayed the possibility of a drastic change in Banco de Mexico's policy of supporting the peso through its method of tightening liquidity in money markets.
Mexico City newspaper El Economista cited unnamed sources at the central bank on Monday as saying that Mexico will avoid lifting interest rates in 1997 to ease pressure on the exchange rate.
In a front page story under a banner headline, the newspaper said that the central bank would aim at keeping interest rates stable in order to allow for a greater increase in "productive activity."

The newspaper said that the increase in net international assets last week to $8.13 billion, after the central bank's payback of $1.5 billion to the International Monetary Fund, would allow it to use reserves to calm any market volatility.
"It sounds rather bizarre to suggest that their spending of reserves would play that role in supporting the currency," said one Mexico City economist who declined to be identified.
The Banco de Mexico also downplayed the report, saying it does not reflect central bank thinking. A spokesman for the central bank said, "It is inaccurate to say the least."
The central bank has not intervened directly in foreign exchange markets with reserves to support the peso since late 1995 and even then it was with relatively small amounts.
For most of 1996 it used tighter liquidity in credit markets to support the currency.
In the outline of its 1997 monetary program, released in late 1996, the central bank acknowledged that it would act to maintain order in the exchange and money markets.

But it said that it would do so by varying levels of internal credit. "Once the conditions that have caused the adjustments in monetary policy have been dissipated, the Banco de Mexico will return to its neutral posture," it said.
But economists said that depending on what causes the volatility in the exchange rate, the central bank could ride out the unrest or try to smooth markets this year.

"There are exchange rate changes that are warranted by economic fundamentals, of the kind we saw in October and November in 1996, and there are the other movements that are not based on fundamentals, like what we saw in October and November 1995," said J.P Morgan economist Alfredo Thorne.

"I think that to the extent that the first type of correction takes place, the central bank should be willing to accept that type of correction, and I think that is what should take place in 1997," he said.
Economists added that using the reserves would only be useful to support a weakening peso if used in conjunction with interest rate increases.
